paragraphs.source_en: The round Head rock paintings of the Central Sahara situated in the Tassili, Tadrart Mountains in Algeria and in the Tadrart Acacus in Libya, represent the earliest paintings created by the Early Holocene huntergatherers. Other forms of rock art, the Kel Essuf engravings representing simple anthropomorphic figures, are located in the same shelters as the Round Head paintings. In the relative chronology the Kel Essuf are older and since they bear common traits with the Round Heads, they may be their predecessors. Bubaline engravings which are very different both stylistically and thematically from the Round Head paintings are mainly concentrated outside the area of the Round Heads which suggests another, possibly competitive, culture at least partially contemporaneous.

paragraphs.source_en: The Pastoral engravings and paintings characteristic for images of domesticated cattle also belong to the prehistoric era. They are attributed to populations of herders who arrived to the Central Sahara in the 8th millennium BP, and their art is found all over the Sahara.

paragraphs.source_en: Previously, the Round Head paintings have mostly been studied as an isolated phenomenon. Their mere description and classification did not bring any conclusion about the art and the population who produced it, the paintings were rarely related to the archaeological record, and rare attempts of interpretation were not accepted. In an effort to advance the research of the Round Heads to a next step, this book proposed a new approach in their study. It is based on the elaboration of information from various scientific fields, namely the archaeology, climatology, landscape archaeology, comparative studies and ethnography, and related to the information from the paintings themselves.
